title: Replace a List Scan with Hashing
subtitle: Why scan every prior file when the existing hash-map insertion already detects duplicates?

metrics.label: CPU cycles
metrics.explanation: Cycles reveal the cumulative cost of repeatedly walking an ever-growing linked list.

metrics.label: Instructions
metrics.explanation: The quadratic scan performs many character comparisons and pointer-following steps.

metrics.label: IPC
metrics.explanation: IPC provides context for the instruction stream; total work is the central evidence here.

metrics.label: Branches
metrics.explanation: Each list node adds loop and string-comparison branches.

metrics.label: Branch-miss rate
metrics.explanation: The rate complements the much larger change in total branch count.

metrics.label: Cache misses
metrics.explanation: Following linked-list nodes can create additional memory-system pressure.

learning.change: The optimized version removes a case-insensitive linked-list scan and lets the already-required hash insertion reject duplicates.
learning.hypothesis: Building n unique entries should drop from quadratic comparison work toward expected linear time.
learning.caution: Hash operations are expected O(1), not guaranteed O(1), and the after version speculatively allocates before discovering a duplicate.
prompts: Why was the linked-list membership check redundant?
How does the speedup change as the directory grows?
Which calling-context metrics distinguish less total work from cache behavior?
When might allocate-then-undo on a duplicate be a poor tradeoff?
